commands.name: alias
commands.summary: Give a command another name for this session.
commands.note: Aliases are lost when the shell exits; put them in ~/.bashrc to keep them. Scripts do not see them.

commands.name: awk
commands.summary: Process text one record (line) at a time, split into fields.

flags.text: Field separator.
The first, second, ... field of the current line; $0 is the whole line.
The number of the current line.
The number of fields on the current line.

commands.note: Examples avoid features only GNU awk has, so they behave the same under mawk and macOS awk.

commands.name: cat
commands.summary: Print files, or join several one after another.

flags.text: Number every output line.

commands.name: cd
commands.summary: Change the current directory of the shell.

flags.text: Go back to the previous directory.
Your home directory (also the default when no argument is given).
The parent directory.

commands.note: A shell builtin: it changes where the shell is, not any file.

commands.name: chmod
commands.summary: Change who can read, write or run a file.

flags.text: Give the owner (u) execute (x) permission. g is group, o is others, a is all.
Octal: owner read and write, everyone else read only.
Octal: owner everything, others read and execute.
Apply to a directory and everything in it.

examples: chmod u+x scripts/hello.sh && ls -l scripts/hello.sh | cut -c1-10 && scripts/hello.sh Ana

commands.name: chown
commands.summary: Change the owner and group of a file. Usually needs sudo.

flags.text: Apply recursively.

commands.note: Not run here: changing ownership needs administrator rights.

commands.name: cp
commands.summary: Copy files and directories.

flags.text: Copy directories recursively (also -R).
Ask before overwriting an existing file.
Never overwrite an existing file.
Print each copy as it happens.
Keep mode, ownership and timestamps.

commands.note: By default cp overwrites an existing destination without asking. -i asks first; -n never overwrites (recent GNU versions warn that its behaviour is non-portable and suggest --update=none).

commands.name: curl
commands.summary: Transfer data from or to a URL.

flags.text: Silent: no progress meter.
Write output to a file instead of the screen.
Save under the name used in the URL.
Follow redirects.
Fetch headers only.
Choose the HTTP method.
Add a request header.
Send data in the request body.

commands.note: Not run here: it needs the network. Never pipe a download straight into a shell (curl ... | bash): you run code you have not read.

commands.name: cut
commands.summary: Cut out columns from each line.

flags.text: Field delimiter (one character).
Which fields to keep, such as 1,3 or 2-4.
Which characters to keep.

commands.name: date
commands.summary: Print or format the date and time.

flags.text: Format: the date as YYYY-MM-DD.
Format: the time as HH:MM:SS.
Use a given date instead of now (GNU; BSD uses -j -f).

commands.note: Examples use a fixed date so the output does not change.

commands.name: df
commands.summary: Show free and used space on mounted file systems.

flags.text: Human-readable sizes.

commands.note: Output depends on the machine, so no example is run.

commands.name: diff
commands.summary: Show the differences between two files.

flags.text: Unified format, the one patches and code review use.
Compare directories recursively.

commands.note: Exit status is 0 when the files are identical, 1 when they differ.

commands.name: du
commands.summary: Show how much disk space files and directories use.

flags.text: Human-readable sizes.
Only a total for each argument.

commands.note: Sizes depend on the file system, so no example is run.

commands.name: echo
commands.summary: Print its arguments.

flags.text: Do not print the trailing newline.
Interpret backslash escapes such as \n (bash). Use printf when you need portability.

examples: echo -n no newline; echo ' ... then this'

commands.name: export
commands.summary: Mark a variable so child processes inherit it.
commands.note: A builtin. The first example shows an exported-less variable is invisible to a child shell.

commands.name: find
commands.summary: Search a directory tree for files by name, type, age or size.

flags.text: Match the file name against a glob such as '*.txt' (quote it).
f for files, d for directories.
Modified N days ago; +N means more than N, -N less than N.
File size, such as +1M.
Do not go deeper than N levels.
Run a command on each match; {} stands for the file and \; ends the command.
Delete every match. Put it last, and run the same find without it first.

commands.note: Without -delete or -exec, find only reads. It lists matches in whatever order the file system gives them, so the examples sort the result.

commands.name: grep
commands.summary: Print lines that match a pattern.

flags.text: Ignore case.
Invert: print lines that do not match.
Show line numbers.
Search directories recursively.
Print only the number of matching lines.
Print only the names of files that match.
Match whole words only.
Use extended regular expressions.
Print only the matching part of each line.
Treat the pattern as a fixed string, not a regular expression.

commands.note: Exit status is 0 if something matched, 1 if nothing did, which scripts use in if statements.

commands.name: head
commands.summary: Print the first lines of a file.

flags.text: How many lines (default 10).

commands.name: history
commands.summary: List the commands you typed earlier.

flags.text: Re-run the last command.
Search your history as you type.

commands.note: Interactive, so it is not run here.

commands.name: kill
commands.summary: Send a signal to a process, by default asking it to terminate.

flags.text: List signal names.
SIGKILL: the process cannot catch it and gets no chance to clean up. Try plain kill first.

commands.name: less
commands.summary: Page through a file one screen at a time.

flags.text: Quit.
Search forward for word; n finds the next match.
Next page.

commands.note: Interactive, so it cannot be run in a page; try it on a long file.

commands.name: ln
commands.summary: Make links between files.

flags.text: Make a symbolic link (a pointer by name) instead of a hard link.

examples: ln -s notes.txt shortcut && cat shortcut | head -n 1

commands.name: ls
commands.summary: List the contents of a directory.

flags.text: Long format: permissions, owner, size and date.
Include hidden entries (names starting with a dot).
With -l, print sizes like 1K or 234M.
Sort by modification time, newest first.
Reverse the sort order.
List subdirectories recursively.
One entry per line.
Sort by size, largest first (GNU and BSD).

commands.note: Colour and column layout depend on your terminal; output here is plain.

commands.name: man
commands.summary: Open the manual page for a command.

flags.text: Search page titles and descriptions for a word.

commands.note: Interactive (it opens a pager). Quit with q. For a short summary, try tldr.

commands.name: mkdir
commands.summary: Create directories.

flags.text: Create missing parent directories, and do not fail if the directory already exists.
Print a line for each directory created.

commands.note: Without -p, creating an existing directory is an error, as the second example shows.

commands.name: mv
commands.summary: Move or rename files and directories.

flags.text: Ask before overwriting.
Never overwrite.
Print each move.

commands.note: Like cp, mv replaces an existing destination silently unless you give -i or -n.

commands.name: ps
commands.summary: List running processes.

flags.text: All users' processes with details (BSD style, no dash).
Every process, full format (POSIX style).

commands.note: Output depends on the machine, so no example is run.

commands.name: pwd
commands.summary: Print the directory the shell is in.

flags.text: Print the physical path, with symbolic links resolved.
Print the logical path (the default).

commands.name: rm
commands.summary: Remove files and directories. There is no recycle bin and no undo.

flags.text: Remove directories and everything in them.
Ignore missing files and never ask. Combined with -r it is the command that empties disks.
Ask before every removal.
Print each removal.
Remove empty directories.

commands.note: Check what a pattern matches before deleting it: run ls with the same pattern first.

commands.name: rmdir
commands.summary: Remove empty directories.

flags.text: Also remove the parent directories, if they become empty.

examples: mkdir empty && rmdir empty && echo removed
commands.note: It refuses to remove a directory that has anything in it, which makes it a safe way to delete.

commands.name: sed
commands.summary: Edit a stream of text, most often to substitute.

flags.text: Print only lines you ask for with p.
Add a script (use it several times).
Use extended regular expressions.
Edit the file in place, overwriting it. BSD/macOS sed needs -i '' (an argument).

commands.note: Without -i it prints the edited text and leaves the file alone.

commands.name: sort
commands.summary: Sort lines.

flags.text: Compare numerically (so 9 sorts before 10).
Reverse the order.
Keep only the first of equal lines.
Sort by a key: field number, such as -k2.
Field separator for -k.

commands.name: sudo
commands.summary: Run one command with administrator rights.
commands.note: Everything the command does, it does with full rights. Read a command twice before putting sudo in front of it, and never pipe a download into sudo bash.

commands.name: tail
commands.summary: Print the last lines of a file.

flags.text: How many lines (default 10).
Keep the file open and print new lines as they are added; stop with Ctrl-C.

commands.name: tar
commands.summary: Bundle files into one archive, and unpack it.

flags.text: Create an archive.
Extract an archive.
List the contents without extracting.
Compress with gzip (use with -c or -x).
Verbose: list files as they are handled.
The archive file name. It must come right before the name.

examples: tar -czf docs.tar.gz docs projects && tar -tzf docs.tar.gz | sort
tar -czf p.tar.gz projects && mkdir out && tar -xzf p.tar.gz -C out && ls out
commands.note: -x overwrites existing files of the same name. Use -t first when you do not know what is inside.

commands.name: tee
commands.summary: Copy standard input to a file and also to standard output.

flags.text: Append to the file instead of overwriting it.

examples: echo hi | tee out.txt && cat out.txt
commands.note: Without -a it overwrites the file.

commands.name: touch
commands.summary: Create an empty file, or update a file's timestamps.

flags.text: Do not create the file if it does not exist.
Use the given date instead of now (GNU; BSD uses -t).

commands.name: tr
commands.summary: Translate or delete characters (reads standard input only).

flags.text: Delete the characters in SET1.
Squeeze repeats of a character into one.

commands.name: type
commands.summary: Say what a name means: builtin, alias, function or program.

flags.text: Show every meaning, not just the first.

commands.note: 'which' is a separate program; 'type' knows about builtins and functions. -t prints just the kind: builtin, file, alias, function or keyword.

commands.name: uniq
commands.summary: Collapse adjacent repeated lines.

flags.text: Prefix each line with how many times it occurred.
Print only lines that were repeated.

commands.note: It only compares neighbouring lines, so sort the input first (the last example shows what happens if you do not).

commands.name: wc
commands.summary: Count lines, words and bytes.

flags.text: Lines only.
Words only.
Bytes only.

commands.name: xargs
commands.summary: Build and run commands from standard input.

flags.text: Use at most N arguments per command.
Replace a placeholder (such as {}) with each input line.
Input is separated by NUL characters, for names with spaces; pair with find -print0.

examples: echo 'a b c' | xargs -n 1 echo item
commands.note: It runs whatever command you give it, so it is as dangerous as that command.
